---
title: Modules
description: How a program's files are named, resolved, compiled, and limited, and which file types and options tenant.load accepts.
---

## Sources

`tenant.load(source, options)` takes one of two sources.

| Source | Main module | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| A string | The string, named by `options.filename` | `filename` defaults to `main.js` |
| `{ main, files }` | `files[main]` | `filename` is refused; `main` must be one of the files |

`files` maps paths to contents. A content is a string or a `Uint8Array`; `load` copies the bytes, so changing the array afterwards doesn't change the program.

Paths are relative, such as `src/index.ts` or `node_modules/hono/package.json`. A leading `./` is removed. A path must not start with `/`, contain empty, `.`, or `..` segments, contain backslashes or control characters, be longer than 1,024 characters, or start with `ext:` or `isolane:`. Two paths that name the same file are refused. Paths become the modules' names in stack traces. Inside the program, each file's path is absolute, under `/`: `src/index.ts` is `/src/index.ts`, and its URL is `file:///src/index.ts`, as [`import.meta`](#importmeta) gives it.

## Resolution

The worker resolves every import over the program's files and nothing else, with [oxc_resolver](https://github.com/oxc-project/oxc-resolver). It never reads the host's filesystem.

| Specifier | Resolves to |
|---|---|
| A relative path, `./routes` | A file of the program. Without an extension, the resolver tries `.ts`, `.tsx`, `.mts`, `.js`, `.jsx`, `.mjs`, and `.json`, then the directory's `index` file. |
| A relative path ending in `.js` or `.mjs` | The `.ts`, `.tsx`, `.js`, or `.jsx` file (for `.js`) or the `.mts` or `.mjs` file (for `.mjs`) of that name, as TypeScript's convention has it |
| A bare specifier, `hono` or `hono/jsx` | A package under `node_modules`, by its `package.json` |
| A pattern in the applicable `tsconfig.json`'s `paths`, `@lib/two` | The file the pattern maps to. See [tsconfig.json](#tsconfigjson). |
| A `file:` URL of one of the program's files, `file:///src/lib/a.js` | That file. A `file:` URL of anything else fails as a missing file. |
| A key of the [`modules` option](/reference/capabilities#modules) | What that option says, before any other rule |
| `isolane:env`, `isolane:files`, `cloudflare:sockets` | The [built-in modules](/reference/guest-environment#built-in-modules) |

A package's `exports` and `imports` fields are matched with these conditions, in this order: `workerd`, `worker`, `browser`, `import`, `default`. This is the order bundlers for Cloudflare Workers use, so a package with a Workers build gets it. A package without `exports` is entered by its `browser`, `module`, or `main` field, in that order, and its `browser` field's aliases apply.

An import that resolves to nothing fails the load with a `TypeError` that names the importing file:

| Import | Error message |
|---|---|
| A missing file | `Cannot find module "./missing.js" imported from a.js` |
| A Node.js built-in, `node:fs` | `Cannot import "node:fs" from a.js: isolane has no Node.js built-in modules; give the program one with the modules option ({ 'node:x': './x.js' }), or read its files with isolane:files` |
| A URL other than a program file's `file:` URL | `Cannot import "https://esm.sh/x" from a.js: only the program's files, isolane:env, isolane:files, cloudflare:sockets, and the modules option's specifiers can be imported` |

Packages must be ES modules. A CommonJS package needs bundling first, as [loading programs](/guides/load-programs#load-a-bundle) shows.

## tsconfig.json

A `tsconfig.json` among the program's files applies its `compilerOptions.paths` and `baseUrl` to imports, with `extends` and project references followed. As TypeScript does, the resolver uses the nearest `tsconfig.json` in the importing file's directory or above it, and none for files under `node_modules`. The file may contain comments and trailing commas.

```json tsconfig.json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "baseUrl": ".",
    "paths": { "@lib/*": ["src/lib/*"], "~config": ["src/config.ts"] }
  }
}
```

With this file, `import { two } from '@lib/two'` loads `src/lib/two.ts`, and `baseUrl` makes `import 'src/lib/three'` load `src/lib/three.ts`.

The `tsconfig` load option changes which file applies:

| `tsconfig` | Effect |
|---|---|
| omitted | The nearest `tsconfig.json` above each importing file |
| a path, `'config/tsconfig.app.json'` | That file, for every import. It must be one of the program's files, or `load` throws `ERR_INVALID_CONFIG`. |
| `false` | No tsconfig file applies |

A tsconfig file that can't be read, such as one whose `extends` names a missing file, fails the load with a `TypeError` that names it. Only `paths` and `baseUrl` are used. Compiler options such as `target`, `jsx`, or `experimentalDecorators` don't change how files compile; the [`ts`](#typescript) and [`jsx`](#jsx) options do.

## Dynamic import

`import()` works for the program's files and the built-in modules, during setup and in calls. A module imported in a call is compiled then, under the call's `cpuMs`. Classic scripts run with `run`, `isolate.eval`, and `isolate.call` can't import; `import()` there rejects with a `TypeError`.

## import.meta

Each module's `import.meta` has the properties Node.js gives it, for the module's path under `/`.

| Property | Value, for `src/index.ts` |
|---|---|
| `url` | `'file:///src/index.ts'`. Characters that URLs escape are escaped: `src/a b.js` is `file:///src/a%20b.js`. |
| `filename` | `'/src/index.ts'` |
| `dirname` | `'/src'` |
| `main` | `true` in the program's main module, `false` in the others |
| `resolve(specifier)` | The URL an import of `specifier` from this module would load, without loading it |

`import.meta.resolve` follows the [resolution](#resolution) rules. For a built-in module or a key of the `modules` option it returns the specifier itself (`'isolane:env'`, `'kv'`). For an import that would fail it throws the `TypeError` the import would fail with, such as `Cannot find module "./nope.js" imported from src/index.js`. Its result can be imported, since a program file's `file:` URL is a specifier:

```js
const { routes } = await import(import.meta.resolve('./routes.js'));
```

`new URL('./data.json', import.meta.url)` names a file beside the module, and [`isolane:files`](/reference/guest-environment#isolanefiles) reads it.

## File types

A file's type comes from its extension, or from an import attribute.

| File | Imports as |
|---|---|
| `.js`, `.mjs` | JavaScript module |
| `.ts`, `.mts` | TypeScript, compiled as described below |
| `.jsx` | JavaScript with JSX |
| `.tsx` | TypeScript with JSX |
| `.json`, or any file `with { type: 'json' }` | The parsed value, as the default export |
| Any file `with { type: 'text' }` | A string, as the default export |
| Any file `with { type: 'bytes' }` | A `Uint8Array`, as the default export |

```ts
import messages from './messages.json';
import readme from './README.md' with { type: 'text' };
import logo from './logo.png' with { type: 'bytes' };
```

The same file imported as two types is two modules.

## TypeScript

The worker compiles TypeScript with [oxc](https://oxc.rs). It doesn't check types.

| `ts` field | Values | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `mode` | `'strip'`, `'transform'` | `'strip'` | `strip` removes types and changes nothing else, as Node.js's type stripping does. `transform` also compiles TypeScript syntax that has runtime behaviour. |
| `experimentalDecorators` | `boolean` | `false` | Legacy decorators. Needs `mode: 'transform'`. |
| `emitDecoratorMetadata` | `boolean` | `false` | TypeScript's decorator metadata. Needs `mode: 'transform'`. |

In `strip` mode, syntax with runtime behaviour fails the load with a `SyntaxError` at that line: enums, namespaces with values, parameter properties, `import x = require()`, and `export =`. The message names `ts: { mode: 'transform' }` as the alternative. Stripping keeps every line and column where it was, so stack positions match the source.

## JSX

JSX in `.jsx` and `.tsx` files is compiled with these `jsx` fields:

| Field | Values | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `runtime` | `'automatic'`, `'classic'` | `'automatic'` | `automatic` imports its functions from `<importSource>/jsx-runtime`. `classic` calls `factory` and `fragment`, which must be in scope. |
| `importSource` | package name | `react` | The automatic runtime's package, resolved in the program's files |
| `factory` | identifier or member expression | `React.createElement` | The classic runtime's element factory |
| `fragment` | identifier or member expression | `React.Fragment` | The classic runtime's fragment |
| `development` | `boolean` | `false` | Use `jsx-dev-runtime` |

## Compile-time constants

`define` replaces expressions in every module at compile time, as esbuild's `define` does. Each key is an identifier or member expression; each value is a string that holds JSON or an identifier or member expression.

```js
await tenant.load(source, { define: { 'process.env.NODE_ENV': '"production"', __DEV__: 'false' } });
```

## Source maps

Stack traces in errors isolane reports point at the original files. This covers `err.guest` on a rejected call or load, `onGuestError`, and the locations of syntax errors. The worker maps positions through:

- the source map of each module it transformed itself;
- a bundle's own map, named by a `//# sourceMappingURL=` comment as a `data:` URL or a path in the program, or a `.map` file beside the bundle with the same name.

Mapping happens in the worker before the error is sent. The guest's own `error.stack` is mapped the same way, when V8 creates it, so a stack a program logs names the same files and lines as the one isolane reports. Deno maps stacks the same way.

A program that sets `Error.prepareStackTrace` receives V8's call sites with their generated positions, which are the compiled code's, not the source's. If that function throws, `error.stack` takes the default, mapped form.

## Limits

| Limit | Default | Maximum | Counts |
|---|---|---|---|
| [`modules`](/reference/limits) | 1,000 | | Files in a program |
| [`moduleBytes`](/reference/limits) | 32 MiB | 64 MiB − 64 KiB | The files' contents and paths together |

A program past either limit fails to load with `ERR_LIMIT`. Parsing, resolving, and transforming happen in the worker, on the instance's thread, so they count against `startupCpuMs` during setup and against a call's `cpuMs` for a later `import()`. The worker keeps transformed modules by content hash, so a program's later instances don't transform its files again; [caches](/concepts/caches) describes what else a worker keeps.
